pr_title: Rewrite profiler notify callbacks into managed
pr_body:
Remove the no longer needed `Thread.InternalGetCurrentThread()`.
Updated generated code to remove passing around `Thread*`.
Converted actual callout into a `QCall`.
No longer emit the "dead" callout code for `QCall`s.
Fixes #50306. https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/50306 is being resolved because it was no repro at this point.
pr_comments: @AaronRobinsonMSFT - Can you help me fill in what connects this change and fixing #50306? I see #50306 talking about slow perf due to GC mode transitions and a stacktrace for a transition caused by MethodTableBuilder::GatherGenericsInfo, but I'm not connecting the dots from that description to this change.

@noahfalk "Fixes" is probably an unfair statement. Perhaps "Closes" is better. Whenever I change code that previously did manual lifetime tracking (that is, FCall, QCall, etc) I run GCStress. I tried to run it and found the issue. I removed the block and it ran without taking an unexpectedly long amount of time on my M2. I'm not taking credit for that improvement here, but since the slow down is no longer present figured it was worth adding it back to the test run. I can add it back if you'd prefer.
@jkotas and @mdh1418 Can you both do one more pass on this. I rewrote a lot this logic and it is now much simpler.

> I'm not taking credit for that improvement here, but since the slow down is no longer present figured it was worth adding it back to the test run. I can add it back if you'd prefer.

I think the change is good how you have it. I'd request instead add a sentence in your commit message and adjust the PR description to clarify the issue no longer reproes but you don't know what the caused the change in behavior.

I was contemplating asking you to run the profiler tests in the diagnostics repo but it appears the only tests which set the COR_PRF_MONITOR_CODE_TRANSITIONS flag are already in the runtime repo. I don't expect running those other diagnostics tests is likely to find anything.
cc @davmason @mdh1418 

Thanks Aaron!

issue_context.body:

comments: I couldn't figure out the best area label to add to this issue. If you have write-permissions please help me learn by adding exactly one [area label](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/area-owners.md).

It is not unusual for certain tests to take too long with GCStress. We mark such tests with `<GCStressIncompatible>true</GCStressIncompatible>`. There are ~700 tests under src\tests marked as such.

> is taking a really long time on Apple Silicon

It may be useful to confirm that it is taking a really long time on other platform too and that this is not Apple Silicon specific issue.

For now I was going to mark it `GCStressIncompatible` for Apple Silicon only.  

I opened the issue because @davmason was surprised it was taking a long time. I can mark it incompatible for all platforms too....

```patch
diff --git a/src/tests/profiler/transitions/transitions.csproj b/src/tests/profiler/transitions/transitions.csproj
index c7b6a7b209a..c387c421362 100644
--- a/src/tests/profiler/transitions/transitions.csproj
+++ b/src/tests/profiler/transitions/transitions.csproj
@@ -5,6 +5,8 @@
     <CLRTestKind>BuildAndRun</CLRTestKind>
     <AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks>
     <CLRTestPriority>0</CLRTestPriority>
+    <!-- Issue https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/50306 -->
+    <GCStressIncompatible Condition="'$(TargetArchitecture)' == 'arm64' and '$(TargetOS)' == 'OSX'">true</GCStressIncompatible>
   </PropertyGroup>
   <ItemGroup>
     <Compile Include="$(MSBuildProjectName).cs" />
```

I don't think there's anything particularly interesting about how this test interacts with gcstress, so it doesn't bother me to disable it, but the test is so simple I have a hard time imagining how it could take an hour without it being a deadlock. It is a very basic test that does one pinvoke and verifies the profiler gets notified.

The profiler tests disables use of use of precompiled code (both `COR_PRF_MONITOR_CODE_TRANSITIONS` and `COR_PRF_DISABLE_INLINING` flags that this test is using will result into disabling use of precompiled code). It means that all code executing during startup gets JITed, and then we trigger stress GC on (almost) every instruction in all that JITed code. It probably should not take a hour, but it won't be fast either.

@sdmaclea Could you plese share full stacktraces of all threads of the process in a gist?
I thought the failure was running under GCStress=3, isn't that just at transitions and other less frequent places?
Hmm, you are right. GCStress=3 should not be too slow.

I can take out the conditions if they are not working correctly, but I do not see this as a good investment of time to fix GCStress for just this test, it is not an interesting scenario

review_comments:
What is a QCall?

Is the idea that this attribute will lead to `PopulateNDirectMethodDescImpl` passing [the condition to set the IsQCall property](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/094649e26a18cd3cdedc7e93a0efabb3da4156b2/src/coreclr/vm/dllimport.cpp#L4396-L4399), so once `CreateNDirectStubAccessMetadata` is hit, the flag bit is toggled and we will always skip notifying the profiler of transitions? Or is it something else that dictates that condition?

It looks like `SF_SkipTransitionNotify` will overrule `CORProfilerTrackTransitions`, do we need `CORProfilerTrackTransitions`? I'm missing the context of when `PopulateNDirectMethodDescImpl` and `CreateNDirectStubAccessMetadata` are invoked, but what are the scenarios in which the `NDIRECTSTUB_FL_SKIP_TRANSITION_NOTIFY` bit won't be set?

A QCall is a normal P/Invoke into the runtime (for example. `coreclr.dll` binary). If you look in `ProfilerManagedToUnmanagedTransitionMD`, you will notice that we don't notify the profiler for QCalls anyways. This change is designed to not even emit the code that is capable of doing the emit if the stub is for a QCall. It was previously unnecessary work that was being done.
